docs.title: The Core Philosophy
docs.text:
• Societal and climate collapse are already underway, so organized, forward-looking groups must engineer community resilience against scarcity and disaster.
  • A realistic, pessimistic outlook on the environment should motivate pragmatic, collective action rather than despair or climate idealism.
  • Political compartmentalization keeps groups focused on practical survival strategies instead of divisive partisan debates.
  • An absolute commitment to reality and evidence-based decision-making is necessary to combat irrationality and conspiratorial thinking.
  • Sub-topics: From Pessimism to Action, A Realistic Pessimistic Outlook, Climate Idealism, Existential Dread and Eco-Emotions, and Cooperation Over Isolation.

docs.title: Introducing Crisis Cadres
docs.text:
• Crisis Cadres are organizations of like-minded individuals collectively focused on providing resilience against whatever form the next crisis takes.
  • They counteract the isolation and distrust bred by scarcity and uncertainty, fostering local self-sufficiency as a buffer against systemic failure.
  • Cadres exist on a continuum, from low-commitment social organizing to fully committed survival groups.
  • Key disciplines include political compartmentalization and an uncompromising commitment to reality (Militant Science).
  • Producing a surplus to share with the wider community is the core recruitment and outreach strategy.

docs.title: The Four Pillars
docs.text:
• The Four Pillars are the core committees: Production, Procurement, Education, and Security.
  • Committee-based governance brings task specialization and decentralized decision-making without bureaucratic inertia.
  • Production creates essential goods, Procurement manages resource flows, Education cultivates skills, and Security protects the endeavor.
  • When approaching a new problem, repeat the mantra: "Have we considered everything through the lens of Production, Procurement, Education, and Security?"
  • The Pillars are interdependent components of a dynamic system, not rigid silos; cadres can mix and match and need not adopt all four.

docs.title: Organizational Strategy and Growth
docs.text:
• Early organizing should begin with simple, low-risk collective projects, such as a bulk staple food purchase, to build trust and demonstrate material benefits.
  • Groups must operate within Dunbar's Number, keeping functional units small to preserve deep social trust.
  • When groups grow beyond human-scale cognitive limits, they should scale through federation rather than centralized bureaucracy.
  • Diversity is a strict strategic imperative that prevents groupthink and enhances problem-solving.
  • Starting a cadre means naming the concrete problem, finding a few committed people, and building trust through small wins.

docs.title: Tactics and Governance
docs.text:
• Governance must be both participatory and decisive, transparent and efficient, avoiding the extremes of bureaucracy and autocracy.
  • Representative government fails through corruption, and pure consensus fails through endless process; cadres strike a balance.
  • Use committee-based representatives while keeping the group under Dunbar's number for agility.
  • Sortition, recallability, Robert's Rules, and bylaws prevent the concentration of power.
  • Subsidiarity and democratic centralism keep decisions local yet unified once made.
  • Operating under the guise of an unremarkable business and collective housing are core tactics for stability.

docs.title: Worldview
docs.text:
• Resilience rests on durable, evidence-based worldviews rather than nationalist myths or religious dogma.
  • Organize human communities in harmony with the land: watersheds, soils, climate, and ecosystems rather than arbitrary political borders.
  • Imperial collapse redistributes suffering and opportunity unevenly, opening space for prepared, principled groups to build more equitable successors.
  • Community and mutual aid, not individual prepping, are the historically proven paths to survival.

docs.title: Praxis Hub
docs.text:
• Praxis Hub is the open-source home of the Crisis Cadres guide, operated on GitHub as a living document.
  • The guide is a well-researched hypothesis to be tested, debated, and improved upon by those serious about doing the work.
  • Anyone can contribute: fix typos, clarify sentences, correct errors, or suggest entirely new sections via pull requests.
  • Field reports and case studies are especially valuable: tell us what worked and what failed spectacularly.
  • The Code of Conduct keeps collaboration disciplined and mission-focused, with political compartmentalization and no personal attacks.
  • The work is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License.
  • The project is a hypothesis that enough people are ready to turn shared anxiety into shared action.

docs.title: The Authors
docs.text:
The Salish Sea Cadre consists of systems thinkers, practical theorists, and advocates for community-led resilience. With a backgrounds in entrepreneurship, engineering, and sustainable systems design, our work focuses on creating actionable frameworks that empower groups to build autonomous, self-sufficient, and equitable futures.

Crisis Cadres is the culmination of years of research and hands-on experimentation, offering a pragmatic roadmap for anyone who believes that the best way to predict the future is to build it ourselves.

docs.title: Example Bylaws
docs.text:
• A model governance charter that codifies the principles of a Crisis Cadre, intended as an adaptable template rather than legal advice.
  • Articles cover name and purpose, membership, governance structure, meetings, committee management, decision-making, core principles, amendments, and dissolution.
  • Admission requires two sponsors, a probationary period, joint vetting, and a two-thirds supermajority vote by secret ballot.
  • Membership is open to those committed to the Cadre's purpose, with a standing obligation to reflect the diversity of its bioregion.
  • The Four Pillars organize all cadre work, with subsidiarity empowering committees within their domains.
  • Officers and committee chairs rotate annually via sortition and remain easily recallable.
  • Democratic centralism, evidence as law, political compartmentalization, bioregionalism, and corporate camouflage are codified as core principles.
  • Amendments require a two-thirds supermajority; dissolution requires a three-fourths vote.

docs.title: Meeting Templates
docs.text:
• Nine adaptable templates aligned with the cadre's core principles of democratic centralism, subsidiarity, and evidence-based action.
  • General Cadre Assembly: the primary monthly meeting for updates and votes on major proposals.
  • New Resilience Project Proposal: structured presentation, debate, and approval of significant new projects.
  • Conflict Resolution and Mediation: a structured, non-adversarial process led by a trained Education mediator.
  • Emergency Response Activation: immediate command-and-control deployment at the onset of a crisis.
  • New Member Integration and Onboarding: welcoming new members and placing them in committees with a mentor.
  • After-Action Review: a non-punitive debrief to identify lessons and improve future performance.
  • Quarterly Strategic Review: SWOT analysis to set clear priorities for the next quarter.
  • New Member Vetting and Vote: confidential consideration of a candidate for admission.
  • Inter-Cadre Confederation Council: coordination, mutual aid, and strategic alignment between allied cadres.
  • Rotate roles like Chair, Secretary, and Timekeeper to distribute responsibility and build experience.

docs.title: Simplified Robert's Rules
docs.text:
• A condensed parliamentary procedure for fair, orderly, and efficient meetings.
  • Core principles: majority rule, minority rights, order and fairness, and one thing at a time.
  • Roles include the Chair, Secretary, Timekeeper, and members.
  • Standard agenda: call to order, minutes, reports, unfinished business, new business, announcements, and adjournment.
  • Motions follow a clear path: move, second, state, debate, vote, announce.
  • Common motions: main motion, amendment, point of order, appeal, table, and adjourn.
  • A majority vote decides most issues; a two-thirds vote is required for major changes such as amending bylaws.[1][2]

docs.text:

docs.title: Cadre Types
docs.text:
• Cadres come in different shapes depending on their emphasis and level of commitment.
  • Procurement heavy: a buying club or buyer's co-op that buys goods in bulk and distributes them to members at a discount.
  • Security only: a neighborhood watch, marksmanship club, or self-defense class that meets to improve member skills.
  • Production heavy: a community garden with a prominent horticulture sub-committee.
  • Shared Nothing: a cadre that shares no physical resources, a low-commitment starting point like a call tree or social club.
  • Fully Employed: all members work for the cadre full-time in lieu of other employment.
  • Full Employment Seeking: a transitional state working toward full employment.
  • Full Housing (Seeking): a cadre where everyone lives in cadre-provided housing, operating like a housing cooperative or land trust.

docs.title: Political Compartmentalization
docs.text:
• Successful resilience requires compartmentalizing divisive political framing while the work of building self-sufficient communities remains deeply political.
  • Culture-war debates, partisan noise, and irrelevant historical disputes drain time and energy and fracture unity.
  • The guiding question for any discussion: does this directly inform a practical resilience strategy?
  • Build, don't grandstand: address injustice by building systems so robust they render old inequalities obsolete, not by perfecting rhetoric.
  • Implement discipline by delegating news monitoring, avoiding clout chasing, and neutralizing disruption tactics.
  • When in doubt, focus on building; without a foundation of survival, there is no ground left on which to fight.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: The Crisis Continuum
docs.text:
• Cadres exist on a continuum, from minor inconveniences on one end to existential threats on the other.
  • On the near end, shared-nothing groups handle routine disruptions such as wildfire smoke or brief power outages.
  • On the far end, fully committed cadres manage dire events, with specialized training required and members engaged around the clock.
  • Cadres adapt their systems to their particular circumstances; recommendations that sound extreme are not prescribed for every context.
  • Degrees of Planning: with global temperatures already near 1.3°C above pre-industrial levels, warming thresholds define what resilience must look like.
  • At 1°C, harden defenses: passive cooling, fire-resistant landscaping, drought-resistant crops, and water capture.
  • At 2°C, pursue radical self-sufficiency: greenhouses, community grain reserves, water as currency, and a possible retreat from coastlines.
  • At 3°C, operate as disaster triage: controlled-environment agriculture, fortified settlements, and clustering in viable zones.
  • At 4°C and beyond, focus on preservation: underground shelters, seed and DNA banks, and the bare blueprint of civilization.
  • The smart money is on preparing for 3°C, bracing for 4°C, and localizing, fortifying, and adapting now.

docs.title: Militant Scientists
docs.text:
• "Militant" signifies an unwavering commitment to reality, not aggression.
  • People spread falsehoods and conspiracies because professing belief serves a social function, not because they believe; fact-checking alone fails.[1][3]
  • Communities that incentivize false witnesses sever their connection to reality, with consequences that compound in crisis.[1][3]
  • False witnesses are a case of costly signaling in humans: the professed belief is a signal of group loyalty, not a claim about the world.[2]
  • Militant Science is a union of rigor and resilience: evidence is sovereign and irrationality is excluded.
  • Evidence hierarchy: peer-reviewed data first, then empirical observation, then provisional expert consensus; speculation and tradition carry little weight.
  • Members may hold personal beliefs, but all cadre-level decisions must be based on testable, evidence-based principles.
  • A cadre that is a monoculture of thought is scientifically weak; diversity of perspective is required for rigor.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Funkhouser, E. (2017). Beliefs as signals: A new function for belief. Philosophical Psychology, 30(6), 809–831. https://doi.org/10.1080/09515089.2017.1291929
  2. Gintis, H., Smith, E. A., & Bowles, S. (2001). Costly signaling and cooperation. Journal of Theoretical Biology, 213(1), 103–119. https://doi.org/10.1006/jtbi.2001.2406
  3. Clark, F. (2008). False witnesses. slacktivist, Patheos. September 8, 2008. https://www.patheos.com/blogs/slacktivist/2008/09/08/false-witnesses/

docs.title: Surplus as Recruitment
docs.text:
• Production should always strive to produce a surplus as a form of recruitment.
  • Having extra to share with the wider community is the most effective way to speak about the cadre and bring its products to those in need.
  • Donating surplus is not charity but strategic outreach that builds trust and attracts new members.
  • A cadre that produces only for itself is merely scraping by; one that intentionally shares grows influence.
  • Surplus goods become bargaining chips in trade, transforming resilience into economic leverage.

docs.title: What Is a Crisis Cadre
docs.text:
• "Cadre" traditionally means a key individual or a trained core group; Crisis Cadres use the term for both, with context clarifying the meaning.
  • A cadre is a highly trained individual or a tightly coordinated group enabling resilient local action.
  • Cadres display leadership, expertise, situational awareness, and the discipline to stay composed in emergencies.
  • The core question of a Crisis Cadre: what are the most likely problems we will encounter, and what actions most increase group resilience against them?
  • Crisis Cadres are egalitarian enterprises that are united, productive, and ever-adapting to overcome adversity.

docs.title: Bylaws and Operating Agreements
docs.text:
• Bylaws codify decision-making processes, voting thresholds, conflict resolution steps, leadership terms, and recall procedures.
  • Bylaws can spell out adding members, handling departures, creating committees, and any other rules the group chooses.
  • When in doubt, bylaws can state that meetings follow a specific edition of Robert's Rules.
  • Operating agreements are always considered private and need not be published, unlike bylaws in certain jurisdictions.
  • Operating agreements are beneficial for cadres following The Corporate Edge.
  • Use concise editions of Robert's Rules and the meeting templates to keep procedures efficient.
  • See the Example Bylaws appendix for a model charter adaptable to your cadre.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: The Corporate Edge
docs.text:
• Small businesses enjoy near-universal goodwill and avoid the ideological reactions triggered by explicitly political projects.
  • A group that organizes as a business can exploit the blind spot of authoritarian systems that tolerate commerce while crushing dissent.
  • The key lies in banality: the more ordinary the business, the more effectively it disappears into the economic landscape.
  • A corporate framework provides built-in stability: bank accounts, contracts, supply chains, and durable legal existence.
  • Structure acts as armor, outlasting individuals and compartmentalizing operations so no single member holds all threads.
  • Preferred sectors include disaster recovery, waste management, agriculture, renewable energy, and medical supplies.
  • Prefer an LLC or corporation over a co-op or non-profit, operating cooperatively through a private operating agreement with temporary appointed figureheads.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
• Representatives and authority figures should be recallable, with the threshold for recall lower than that of nomination.
  • Distribute committee assignments evenly so no one is overloaded and no committee is empty.
  • Sortition, or drawing lots, randomly assigns key roles and committee positions to prevent stratification.
  • Democratic centralism: full and open debate before a decision, then unified support and implementation once decided.
  • Give significant weight to the findings of specialized, evidence-based committees once ratified.
  • Leadership becomes a temporary duty or service, not a path to personal power.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Housing
docs.text:
• Housing is the largest single financial drain for most members and the cornerstone of personal and collective security.
  • Embrace smaller, more efficient living spaces so resources stretch further and housing can be secured in a single communal acquisition.
  • Phase One, immediate solutions: strategic re-appropriation, hidden dwellings, leveraging zoning loopholes, and low-investment shelters.
  • Phase Two, the housing rollup: Procurement acquires a property and rents it at cost, with surplus reinvested to pay down principal.
  • Phase Three, integrated communities: greenhouse villages, agrihoods, reclaimed urban space, and deconstruction of derelict structures for materials.
  • Surplus housing becomes a strategic tool for outreach, offering safe temporary shelter to allies and growing the movement.
  • Advanced cadres can use strategic acquisitions and coordinated migration to influence local government and revitalize struggling towns.

docs.title: Subsidiarity
docs.text:
• Decisions should be made at the lowest competent and practical level, by those most directly affected by and knowledgeable about an issue.
  • Local knowledge leads to better solutions; a production committee understands its challenges better than a centralized council.
  • Empowering local committees prevents every minor action from passing through slow layers of approval.
  • Decentralization fosters ownership and accountability among those who shape the decisions that affect them.
  • To break a tie, weigh the opinions of those closest to the issue and the relevant expertise.

docs.title: Climate Idealism
docs.text:
• Many well-meaning climate-concerned groups waste energy on weak actions like awareness-raising protests and small personal gestures.
  • Individual choices, such as metal straws or going vegan, are worthwhile but woefully inadequate against centuries of industrial destruction.
  • Reversing emissions at scale would require building all existing oil and gas infrastructure in reverse.
  • Cadres prioritize survivability over sustainability; sustainability emerges naturally from a posture of resilient survivalism.
  • Cadres still champion electrification and large-scale mitigation, but do not assume meaningful global mitigation will be achieved.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Cooperation Over Isolation
docs.text:
• The path away from dread and toward self-determination runs through small, local groups.
  • Groups centered on a tangible goal, such as practical resilience, bring people together across ideological divides.
  • Small groups allow trust to develop gradually through shared work, creating natural opportunities for relationships.
  • Resilience building is actionable at the local level and needs no political consensus or institutional approval.
  • Over time, small networks grow, interlink, and form the foundation of a broader resilience strategy through federation.
  • No one is truly prepared alone; cooperation is a lived reality, not an abstract ideal.

docs.title: Existential Dread and Eco-Emotions
docs.text:
• Existential dread is not new, but today it is amplified by globalized risks: climate disasters, mass extinctions, AI, pandemics, political instability, and societal collapse.[1]
  • A 2021 global survey of 10,000 young people aged 16–25 across 10 countries found 75% said the future is frightening, and over half question whether having children is ethical.[1]
  • "Solastalgia," emotional distress caused by environmental change, is a hidden toll of collapse.[2]
  • Research shows not all eco-emotions are equal: anger is the most adaptive response, linked to better mental health and more climate action.[3]
  • Anxiety and depression are less adaptive and often lead to disengagement.[3]
  • The goal is to move from grief and anxiety to anger, and from anger to collective action.

docs.text:

The Lancet Planetary Health, 5(12), e863–e873. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2542-5196(21)00278-3
  2. Albrecht, G. (2007). Solastalgia: the distress caused by environmental change. Australasian Psychiatry, 15(S1), S95–S98. https://doi.org/10.1080/10398560701701288
  3. Stanley, S. K., Hogg, T. L., Leviston, Z., & Walker, I. (2021). From anger to action: Differential impacts of eco-anxiety, eco-depression, and eco-anger on climate action and wellbeing. The Journal of Climate Change and Health, 1, 100003. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joclim.2021.100003

docs.title: From Pessimism to Action
docs.text:
• Optimism requires confronting reality before acting.
  • Jem Bendell's 2018 paper "Deep Adaptation" argues climate change is irreversible and near-term societal collapse is either likely, inevitable or already unfolding, while critiquing sustainability efforts as insufficient.[1]
  • Bendell was once dismissed as alarmist, but subsequent climate data and events have proven him largely correct, with many measures exceeding predictions.
  • Even if the worst projections are wrong, preparedness pays off: if we are ready for the worst, we can face coming crises and help others.
  • Maintaining a realistic pessimistic outlook best informs rational decisions about the future.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bendell, J. (2018). Deep Adaptation: A Map for Navigating Climate Tragedy. IFLAS Occasional Paper 2. Institute for Leadership and Sustainability, University of Cumbria. https://www.lifeworth.com/deepadaptation.pdf

docs.title: A Realistic Pessimistic Outlook
docs.text:
• Climate change is irreversible; even if all emissions stopped today, feedback mechanisms would continue warming the earth.
  • Mass species extinction will accelerate in our lifetimes, and we should be mentally and materially prepared for it.
  • With few exceptions, governments will fail to address these challenges due to regulatory capture and corruption.
  • Attempted policy changes and panic responses will often make things worse, wasting resources on misguided mitigation.
  • Wars will intensify and consume more fossil fuels, and no technological fix will materialize in time.
  • Plan for every easily extractable drop of oil to be consumed, and for "successful" mitigations and efficiency gains to be undone or absorbed.
  • Climate-concerned groups risk wasting energy on climate idealism rather than effective action.
  • The only realistic tool available is local adaptation, prioritizing survivability over sustainability.

docs.title: Beyond the Core Four
docs.text:
• An anti-fragile posture requires specialized committees tailored to a community's unique circumstances and evolving needs.
  • Common committee areas include Health and Wellness, Housing and Infrastructure, Transportation and Logistics, Communication and Technology, Ecology and Land Stewardship, Hospitality and Integration, and Scavenger and Salvage.
  • Committee models differ by function: investigative, special purpose and spin-off, empowered, limited-function, and hybrid.
  • New committees must form democratically from identified needs, pilot temporarily, and rotate roles to prevent burnout.
  • Learn from local disasters to pinpoint gaps, and let members contribute to multiple committees based on capacity.
  • Resilience is a living experiment: start with the Four Pillars, stay flexible, and let necessity guide innovation.

docs.title: Education
docs.text:
• Education is the cadre's living mind: it asks what the group must know and ensures critical skills are deeply embedded, widely shared, and constantly evolving.
  • Core responsibilities include knowledge preservation, conflict resolution, outreach, media relations, and credentialing.
  • Education identifies skill gaps and designs tiered programs to fill them, in partnership with Security for critical skills.
  • Cadres should cultivate a reputation as extremely learned and experienced: able to suture wounds, plant corn, mediate conflict, and balance books.
  • Media relations default to silence, and the cadre's story is told on its own terms through controlled channels.
  • Sub-topics: Education Fundamentals, Media Narratives and Information Sovereignty, and Essential Skills and Credentialing.

docs.title: Essential Skills and Credentialing
docs.text:
• The true currency of resilience is demonstrable, practiced mastery, not abstract knowledge or superficial familiarity.
  • Traditional merit badges reward effort and participation over real expertise, which is dangerously insufficient for adult cadres.
  • A cadre credentialing system must verify proven competence under real-world conditions.
  • Credentials require consistent, reliable performance over seasons or project cycles, not a single attempt.
  • Mastery includes the ability to teach and mentor others, ensuring skills become part of collective capacity.
  • Example credentials include poultry husbandry, food preservation, blacksmithing, renewable energy systems, and community defense.
  • Credentials should be subject to periodic reassessment so skills do not atrophy.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Education Fundamentals
docs.text:
• Education preserves culture and knowledge: oral histories, traditional skills, indigenous wisdom, and community seed banks.
  • It handles internal friction before it escalates through mediation, counseling, and training in non-violent communication.
  • Managing burnout and mental health is core to Education, protecting against the attrition of long-term collapse.
  • Outreach is traditional "marketing": public workshops spread knowledge and double as talent scouting for new members.
  • Maintain a secure, self-hosted "Praxis Hub" for documents, remote meetings, and coordination.
  • Prevent knowledge hoarding through mentorship, peer-to-peer teaching, and inter-committee skill sharing.
  • Rotate positions and share information across all roles, so balanced jobs prevent a permanent underclass and redundancy ensures no skill is lost.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Media Narratives and Information Sovereignty
docs.text:
• Journalists hunt for spectacle, clickbait, and profitable headlines; their motivations almost never align with the cadres.
  • The default position with respect to the media should be silence.
  • Route questions through controlled channels, answered only in formats the cadre dictates.
  • Interviews should be rare and only through elected spokespeople trained in deflection and steering conversations back to solid ground.
  • The cadre's story is best told on its own terms, in its own spaces.
  • Correct only the gravest lies and move on; leave trolls to starve.

docs.title: Procurement
docs.text:
• Procurement is the circulatory system of the community, managing the flow of material, financial, and informational resources.
  • It scales along the continuum from "what does everyone want for lunch" to full-time property, fund, accounting, and legal management.
  • Core duties include buying plans, purchasing, taxes, supplier management, inventory tracking, budgeting, compliance, logistics, and resource sharing.
  • The audit is a core function that shifts Procurement from a passive buyer into an architect of resilience.
  • Financial uplifting and enhanced financial strategies build a cadre wealth fund while raising the security of its most vulnerable members.
  • Sub-topics: Procurement Fundamentals, The Audit, Financial Uplifting, and Enhanced Financial Strategies.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: The Audit
docs.text:
• By analyzing receipts and purchase records, Procurement spots recurring expenditures and asks the critical question: could we produce this ourselves?
  • Poll committees, individuals, and receipts to determine where the group's money is going.
  • If vegetables come from distant suppliers, expand gardens or invest in greenhouses; if repairs drain funds, organize workshops to build those skills.
  • Bring these insights to the wider community to democratize decisions on where to invest in local capacity.
  • The audit shifts Procurement from a passive buyer to an architect of resilience, always seeking dual-win recommendations that lower costs while increasing resilience.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Enhanced Financial Strategies
docs.text:
• Invest idle cadre funds in safe options like short-term bonds to preserve capital and earn a modest yield, the seed of a sovereign wealth fund.
  • Borrow against collective assets such as real estate or equipment to fund large projects or bridge cash flow gaps.
  • Establish structured internal lending for member needs, complemented by local currencies or time banks.
  • Minimize taxes through strategic planning, write-offs, and member education delivered with Education.
  • Acquire grants for climate resilience projects, such as solar microgrids and rainwater harvesting, to leapfrog financial constraints.

docs.title: Financial Uplifting
docs.text:
• A cadre cannot thrive if members are trapped in financial hardship.
  • A member with weak or no credit provides a card that Procurement uses to purchase group resources, paying the balance off immediately through collective dues.
  • Reimbursements are processed instantly with written documentation, removing any risk to the cardholder.
  • Over time this system systematically improves the credit of the most financially vulnerable members.
  • This mirrors fraternal organizations such as the Shriners, Freemasons, and Elks, who thrived by offering members economic advantages.
  • This advanced strategy carries real risks and should only be attempted by mature cadres with airtight operating agreements and mutual trust.

docs.title: Procurement Fundamentals
docs.text:
• Procurement transforms scarcity into strategic advantages and logistical hurdles into opportunities for connection.
  • Buying plans for beneficial goods are proposed and voted on by the cadre, ensuring collective oversight and preventing wasteful spending.
  • All purchases flow through Procurement unless another committee is explicitly authorized for special cases.
  • Maintain a vetted supplier database evaluated on reliability, ethics, and backup options.
  • Track inventory in real time, anticipating needs and managing discreet, decentralized caches of critical supplies.
  • Oversee transportation, storage, and fair distribution, and run tool libraries and skill exchanges so no resource sits idle.

docs.title: Production
docs.text:
• Production turns raw materials, labor, and knowledge into the essentials of life: food, water, shelter, energy, tools, and medicine.
  • A community that cannot produce is perpetually one crisis away from collapse.
  • "Appropriate Production" means making what is needed, with what is available, without waste, prioritizing low-energy, small-scale output.
  • Production exists on a continuum, from mending clothes and growing herbs to a full-employment, self-sustaining economy.
  • A cadre that produces a surplus to share transforms resilience into recruitment and economic leverage.
  • Sub-topics: Production Fundamentals, Food Production and Security, Equipment Fabrication and Restoration, Energy and Utilities, Medicine and Hygiene, Automation, and The Resilience Premium.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
• Do not dismiss AI and robotics; natural human language can now command real-world actions from machines, revitalizing robotics.
  • Open-source models and affordable hardware make capable automation increasingly accessible to serious organized groups.
  • A robot working around the clock is a force multiplier for weeding, planting, harvesting, patrolling, and repair.
  • Small groups can achieve high self-sufficiency and decouple from fragile supply chains without soul-crushing labor.
  • Refusing the technology leaves a group at the mercy of those who wield it; control efforts by states and corporations are likely porous.
  • Procurement monitors the market, Education maintains the skills, and Security ensures proper safeguards.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Energy and Utilities
docs.text:
• Energy is the backbone of every other pillar; food, shelter, and security all depend on reliable power.
  • Decentralized energy reduces vulnerability: solar panels, micro-hydro, wind turbines, and biogas digesters fit well within appropriate production.
  • Maintain manual backups such as hand pumps, wood stoves, and mechanical tools so a lack of electricity is not a single point of failure.
  • Small-scale storage and efficiency habits reduce dependence on an unstable grid.
  • Redundant, decentralized systems ensure the failure of a single node cannot black out the community.

docs.title: Equipment Fabrication and Restoration
docs.text:
• A society built on disposable goods is perpetually at the mercy of those who sell them.
  • A basic workshop, a place for repairs, is the logical first step: sewing machines mend torn fabric and soldering irons resurrect electronics.
  • Beyond repair lies fabrication: blacksmiths and machinists turn scrap metal into usable parts, and 3D printers craft replacements locally.
  • Where new materials are scarce, salvage becomes an art: old barrels become rainwater collectors, pallets become shelving, and broken appliances yield wire, gears, and motors.
  • Very little is truly waste; think of it as raw material waiting to be reshaped.

docs.title: Food Production and Security
docs.text:
• A cadre that depends on grocery stores is one bad harvest, shipping delay, or economic shock away from hunger.
  • Prioritize calorie-dense staples like potatoes, beans, and grains for immediate survival needs.
  • Balance emergency preparedness with long-term planning such as perennials and permaculture.
  • Use climate-resilient methods: greenhouses, drought-resistant crops, and rainwater harvesting to buffer unpredictable weather.
  • Extend harvests through preservation: canning, fermenting, and drying.
  • Explore aquaponics and hydroponics for intensive, space-efficient production and small-scale animal husbandry for diverse food and skills.
  • Volunteering farm labor builds goodwill, strengthens local food networks, and provides hands-on learning.
  • Ask: if the trucks stopped rolling tomorrow, how long could we feed ourselves?

docs.title: Production Fundamentals
docs.text:
• The ability to produce life's necessities is the bedrock of true independence.
  • Production focuses relentlessly on essentials: food, water, shelter, energy, tools, and medicine, before anything else.
  • Avoid financialized and detached activities, such as crypto schemes, influencer culture, and endless consulting, that generate revenue but not survival value.
  • The results of production must serve a clear, cadre-determined purpose rather than decoration.
  • The goal is always the same: move from dependency to self-sufficiency, one step at a time.

docs.title: Medicine and Hygiene
docs.text:
• A health crisis can unravel a community faster than any shortage of food.
  • A medicinal garden is the first line of defense: yarrow for wounds, willow bark for pain, garlic and elderberry for immunity.
  • Cultivate medicinal and gourmet mushrooms to support health and food security.
  • Soap-making and alcohol distillation ensure sanitation, while composting toilets turn waste from a problem into a resource.
  • Stocked first aid kits with sutures, tourniquets, and antibiotics can make all the difference when needed.

docs.title: The Resilience Premium
docs.text:
• Unlike profit-driven systems, cadres can prioritize resilience over revenue.
  • The products of resilience do not need to compete with products sold on global markets.
  • Any difference in price can be considered a resilience premium: the value of local availability when you need something in times of scarcity.
  • Resilience can be built as a vocation or side project, free of the constraints of profitability.
  • There may be times funds are absolutely needed to keep operations going, but there are times when resilience is its own reward.
  • Production is the antidote to dependency: the steady act of making sure that when external systems fail, the cadre does not.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Security graduates from basic preparedness to a professionalized community defense model as circumstances require.
  • It starts with mundane foundations: call trees, neighborhood watch, site hardening, and pest control.
  • Core duties include asset protection, OPSEC, self-defense training, and operational discipline.
  • The emphasis is on deterrence and defense, never offensive force; cadres are not expeditionary raiding forces.
  • Advanced cadres study modern conflicts and harden against real threats while fostering a culture of confident preparedness.
  • Sub-topics: Security Fundamentals, Defensive Strategy, Weapons and Legal Defense, and OPSEC and Communication Resilience.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Defensive Strategy
docs.text:
• Study recent military conflicts without glorifying war, focusing strictly on the material factors behind success and failure.
  • Cheap and plentiful consumer-grade drones have become the largest cause of battlefield casualties; countermeasures may become critical, depending on your position in the crisis continuum.
  • Successful defensive strategies spread out resources, use earth-bermed or semi-subterranean structures, and manage the group's profile.
  • Going at least partially underground offers dual wins: protection and cheap temperature stabilization against extreme heat.
  • Deterrence comes from visible competence and organization, rather than posturing.
  • Security should control the narrative and terrain in a high-threat scenario, but offensive conquest is always off the table.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Security Fundamentals
docs.text:
• Security begins with practical prevention: auditing spaces, installing lights, reinforcing locks, and delineating private and communal areas.
  • Protect the products of Production and Procurement from theft, spoilage, and pests through locked storage and integrated pest management.
  • Every member should have at least some security training to prevent a "warrior caste" from forming.
  • Establish a clear chain of command in the field, even in otherwise horizontal organizations.
  • Run scenario-based crisis simulations until responses are reflexive and fear is overridden by training.
  • The goal is not a paranoid fortress but a culture of confidence through competence.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: OPSEC and Communication Resilience
docs.text:
• When the social contract begins to fray, maintain operational security for group resources and plans.
  • Use encrypted messaging, code words, and proper password hygiene for shared digital assets.
  • Establish redundant communication networks: radio, runners, and organized observation protocols.
  • Train members in cybersecurity, encrypted communication tools, mesh networks, and radio operation.
  • Seemingly simple actions, such as securely managing passwords for common accounts, are part of Security's mandate.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Weapons and Legal Defense
docs.text:
• Train with the most effective defensive tools that are legally available in your jurisdiction.
  • Certain tools can kill and must be treated with extreme respect, stored securely, and used only as a last resort in defense of life.
  • De-escalation is always the primary goal.
  • Statistically, firearms are much more likely to cause harm to the owner than provide protection, especially in high-stress situations.
  • Maintain an armory under lock and key, with access scaled to the situation along the crisis continuum.
  • Armory operation and maintenance is an instrumental goal for Security.

docs.title: Praxis Hub
docs.text:
• Praxis Hub is the open-source home of the Crisis Cadres guide, operated on GitHub as a living document.
  • The guide is a well-researched hypothesis to be tested, debated, and improved upon by those serious about doing the work.
  • Anyone can contribute: fix typos, clarify sentences, correct errors, or suggest entirely new sections via pull requests.
  • Field reports and case studies are especially valuable: tell us what worked and what failed spectacularly.
  • The Code of Conduct keeps collaboration disciplined and mission-focused, with political compartmentalization and no personal attacks.
  • The work is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License.
  • The project is a hypothesis that enough people are ready to turn shared anxiety into shared action.

docs.title: Organizational Strategy and Growth
docs.text:
• Early organizing should begin with simple, low-risk collective projects, such as a bulk staple food purchase, to build trust and demonstrate material benefits.
  • Groups must operate within Dunbar's Number, keeping functional units small to preserve deep social trust.
  • When groups grow beyond human-scale cognitive limits, they should scale through federation rather than centralized bureaucracy.
  • Diversity is a strict strategic imperative that prevents groupthink and enhances problem-solving.
  • Starting a cadre means naming the concrete problem, finding a few committed people, and building trust through small wins.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Adding Members
docs.text:
• Membership processes commonly include sponsorship, vetting, voting thresholds, and probationary periods.
  • Most elite groups require a sponsor, and many require two current members to nominate a candidate.
  • Vetting may include background checks, interviews, and waiting periods, as with the Freemasons or Augusta National.
  • Admission thresholds range from a simple majority to unanimous consent; many groups require a supermajority.
  • Make it easier to remove a member than to admit one, echoing the principle of recallability.
  • Probationary periods give prospective members a trial membership and a chance to contribute.
  • Make prospective members feel welcome and integrate them into active projects immediately.
  • Diversity is non-negotiable when adding members.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Praxis 101: The Bulk Buy
docs.text:
• A single pooled purchase of a staple food is the repeatable first project that teaches the Cadre model through action, not discussion.
  • The proposal must be specific, low-risk, and offer an undeniable advantage over individual effort.
  • Assign small teams for the functions of the Four Pillars: money and logistics, division and processing, communication, and storage.
  • Keep the money simple so everyone contributes the same amount and the ledger is transparent.
  • Conduct an after-action review with evidence-based questions before introducing any theory.
  • No grounding in theory of any kind is required to get started; trust, cohesion, and competence are byproducts of the exercise.

docs.title: Diversity as a Strategic Imperative
docs.text:
• Diversity is a pragmatic imperative for survival and antifragility, not tokenism or quotas.
  • Diverse teams solve complex problems better through a broader range of perspectives and experience.
  • A resilient cadre mirrors the demographics of its bioregion, or actively seeks global perspectives where local diversity is limited.
  • Homogeneity must be justified and accompanied by a plan to correct the imbalance.
  • Integration, not tokenism: distribute leadership, rotate decision-making power, and ensure all voices shape the cadre's direction.
  • Think of diversity as risk management: a human polyculture thrives under stress where a monoculture fails.

docs.title: Dunbar's Number and Scaling
docs.text:
• Human groups function optimally below approximately 150 members; beyond that, trust and cohesion degrade.
  • Social relationships exist in layers: a core of five intimate bonds, fifteen close, fifty cooperative, and a maximum of 150.
  • Small groups rely on trust, reputation, and peer accountability rather than rigid rules and enforcement.
  • Keep core committees to 15 to 20 active members for focused work, and the entire cadre under 150.
  • Dunbar's Number is a design principle, not a rigid cap, that keeps relationships real and mutual support a lived reality.[1]

docs.text:
1. Dunbar's number. Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunbar%27s_number

docs.title: Early Activities and Shared Concerns
docs.text:
• Organize around disaster preparedness with something easy like a neighborhood call tree for redundant coverage.
  • Ask the shared questions: do we have enough to eat if stores close, enough clean water, and support for the elderly and disabled?
  • Schedule regular meetings and organize potlucks; Procurement determines who brings what and Production makes the meal.
  • Form sub-committees for specific projects, such as a Horticulture sub-committee under Production for a community garden.
  • Potatoes are a great starter crop: resilient, calorie-rich, and difficult to mess up.
  • Start now, since growing methods can take multiple seasons to perfect in your context.
  • Stop worrying about when things will happen and act; shared needs are the organizing focus.

docs.title: Federation and Confederation
docs.text:
• Beyond Dunbar's limit, encourage the formation of new semi-autonomous cadres rather than a monolithic bureaucracy.
  • Cadres confederate through shared principles and protocols, mutual aid pacts, and common operational standards.
  • Rotating delegates form a council for inter-cadre coordination, preventing the permanent centralization of power.
  • Modular redundancy means the failure of one cadre does not collapse the network.
  • This federated model mirrors the Iroquois Confederacy, certain anarchist collectives, and cooperative networks like Mondragon.

docs.title: From Spark to Flame
docs.text:
• Building a cadre starts with naming what is actually broken in your corner of the world and what better would look like.
  • Find your people: a few committed individuals with different skills beat a crowd of half-hearted ones.
  • Agree on basics before acting: how decisions get made, what is off-limits, and whether resources are shared.
  • Start small and build trust through low-stakes wins like a bulk order or group meetup.
  • Formalize light structure around the Four Pillars without soul-crushing bureaucracy.
  • Build culture deliberately: rituals, recognition, and nimble decision-making keep a group alive.
  • Keep under the magic 150 and spin off new cadres to grow without losing your soul.

docs.title: Worldview
docs.text:
• Resilience rests on durable, evidence-based worldviews rather than nationalist myths or religious dogma.
  • Organize human communities in harmony with the land: watersheds, soils, climate, and ecosystems rather than arbitrary political borders.
  • Imperial collapse redistributes suffering and opportunity unevenly, opening space for prepared, principled groups to build more equitable successors.
  • Community and mutual aid, not individual prepping, are the historically proven paths to survival.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: Bioregional Design
docs.text:
• Political borders are arbitrary liabilities that rarely align with the planet's natural systems.
  • A bioregion is defined by watersheds, ecosystems, climate zones, geology and soil, and topography.
  • Organizing along bioregional lines makes water a shared responsibility and aligns agriculture with the land, reducing chemical inputs and supply chain reliance.
  • Be pragmatic about purity: with a changing planet, assisted migration of species from other bioregions can be the most resilient choice.
  • Growth follows the land's carrying capacity; a cadre that outgrows a watershed splits along natural seams.
  • Trade within and between bioregions is purposeful and reciprocal, born of mutual benefit rather than extraction.
  • Bioregionalism is an antidote to the poison of nationalism.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: The Individualist Illusion
docs.text:
• Lone-wolf prepping is a symptom of the competitive alienation and atomization that contribute to systemic fragility.
  • Prepping has become a commodified anxiety, marketed through influencers, gear companies, and dystopian fiction.
  • No individual or single family can possess all the skills or stockpile enough resources to endure a prolonged collapse alone.
  • An isolated, well-stocked haven becomes an attractive target for desperate, organized groups.
  • Prolonged isolation under duress has severe psychological consequences.
  • History demonstrates that survival through crisis is a product of collective action and mutual aid.
  • Real endurance is found in the strength of one's community, not the depth of one's bunker.

Start a discussion · View discussions · Edit this page

docs.title: When Empires Fall
docs.text:
• Civilizations rise, flourish, decline, and collapse in recurring cycles through human history.
  • Imperial collapse is not an unmitigated catastrophe; it can bring liberation for the enslaved, heavily taxed, and colonized.
  • From Rome to the Maya to colonial powers, collapse often produces more decentralized, egalitarian social forms.
  • Collapse redistributes suffering and opportunity unevenly, and those aligned with the old power structure face dispossession.
  • Cadres should prepare to weather short-term chaos while positioning themselves to shape a more equitable successor society.
  • Focus on local resilience that endures the storm and serves as a seed for a more just future.
